q: Define rotator cuff tendinopathy in one sentence.
a: A painful, load-related disorder of the rotator cuff tendons and the tissues immediately around them, in which the demand placed on the tendon has exceeded its capacity to tolerate that demand.

q: Which term is currently preferred in much of the literature, and why?
a: Rotator cuff-related shoulder pain (RCRSP). It is a broader clinical term covering pain associated with the cuff and surrounding subacromial structures, without claiming to know which tissue is responsible.

q: What does "subacromial pain syndrome" (SAPS) describe?
a: Shoulder pain associated with the subacromial region, without necessarily identifying a specific tissue as the source.

q: Why has "subacromial impingement syndrome" fallen out of use?
a: It implies mechanical compression of subacromial tissues as the cause — now considered an incomplete explanation of rotator cuff-related pain, and undermined by placebo-controlled surgical trials.

q: Why is structural abnormality on imaging an unreliable guide to symptoms?
a: Pain is multifactorial. Structural abnormalities identified on imaging do not always correlate with symptoms — they are common in people with no shoulder pain at all.

q: In which populations is rotator cuff tendinopathy most common?
a: Adults who perform repetitive lifting, overhead activities or physically demanding work. It affects daily activities, sleep, occupational performance and sport.

q: What is the central mechanism by which symptoms develop?
a: Demands placed on the shoulder exceed its current capacity — through a sudden increase in activity, repetitive loading with insufficient recovery, or gradual decline in tendon and muscle capacity.

q: Name the two directions in which a capacity–load mismatch can arise.
a: Load rises (new job, return to sport, DIY project) or capacity falls (detraining, illness, a break from activity). Returning to a previous level after a layoff combines both.

q: Why does a "return to normal activity after a break" so often trigger symptoms?
a: The patient returns to an old load with a detrained shoulder. They report nothing new, because in their mind nothing changed.

q: Which systemic factors raise the risk or worsen the course?
a: Diabetes and poor glycaemic control, smoking, sleep disturbance, thyroid disease, weight and mood. These form the "hostile background" to treat as part of the plan.

q: Name the four rotator cuff muscles and their principal actions.
a: Supraspinatus (abduction, compression), infraspinatus (external rotation), teres minor (external rotation), subscapularis (internal rotation). All four compress the humeral head into the glenoid.

q: What is the rotator cable?
a: A thickened band of fibres running perpendicular to the supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons, spanning from the biceps anchor anteriorly to the inferior infraspinatus posteriorly.

q: What is the crescent, and why does the cable–crescent arrangement matter clinically?
a: The crescent is the thinner tissue the cable spans. If the cable remains intact, load is transmitted around rather than through a crescent defect — which is why some tears remain functional.

q: What is the enthesis, and why is it a common site of tear initiation?
a: The graded transition between tendon and bone. It exists to spread stress across a junction between materials of vastly different stiffness, which makes it a stress concentrator.

q: Why does surgical repair not restore the enthesis?
a: It heals with fibrovascular scar, which is weaker. This is the biological reason behind re-tear rates and the three-month delay before strengthening after repair.

q: What is the rotator interval and what does it contain?
a: The triangular gap between the anterior border of supraspinatus and the superior border of subscapularis. It contains the coracohumeral ligament, the superior glenohumeral ligament, and the long head of biceps.

q: What forms the biceps pulley?
a: The coracohumeral ligament, superior glenohumeral ligament and subscapularis insertion — a sling holding the long head of biceps in its groove.

q: A medially subluxed long head of biceps on ultrasound indicates what?
a: A subscapularis lesion — not an isolated biceps problem.

q: How should the long head of biceps be regarded in cuff disease?
a: As a companion diagnosis, not a competing one. It is richly innervated, frequently inflamed alongside cuff disease, and a common reason anterior shoulder pain persists after the cuff settles. Test with Speed's and palpation in the groove with the arm in 10° internal rotation.

q: What forms the coracoacromial arch, and what passes beneath it?
a: The acromion, the coracoacromial ligament and the coracoid process. Beneath pass the supraspinatus tendon, the long head of biceps and the bursa.

q: What is the normal acromiohumeral interval, and what does narrowing indicate?
a: Normally 7–14 mm. Below 7 mm indicates superior migration of the humeral head — a marker of a large or massive tear, not simple tendinopathy.

q: What is the real function of the subacromial–subdeltoid bursa?
a: To allow the cuff to glide under the arch with minimal friction. It is the largest bursa in the body, synovial, capable of thickening and effusion, and a significant pain source.

q: Why does fluid in both the joint and the bursa suggest a full-thickness tear?
a: The bursa does not normally communicate with the glenohumeral joint.

q: Where does a subacromial injection go, and why?
a: Into the bursa, never into the tendon. The bursa is the synovial, innervated structure being targeted.

q: What does narrowing of the subacromial space during elevation signify?
a: Nothing pathological. The space narrows physiologically during elevation, including in asymptomatic shoulders.

q: What are the critical shoulder angle thresholds?
a: Greater than 35° is associated with cuff tears; less than 30° with glenohumeral osteoarthritis.

q: What is the status of neovascularity as a treatment target?
a: Not a target. It is found in asymptomatic tendons, absent in many symptomatic ones, and treatments aimed at ablating neovessels have not produced convincing or durable results. Report it; don't build the plan on it.

q: What problem does the shoulder have to solve mechanically?
a: It has the largest range of motion in the body and almost no passive stability — a large humeral head on a shallow glenoid, with a capsule that is lax through mid-range. Something must pay that bill actively, every second the arm is in use.

q: Define concavity-compression.
a: The cuff compresses the convex humeral head into the concave glenoid. Pressing a ball into a socket makes the socket resist the ball sliding out — the deeper the socket and the harder you press, the more shear force it takes to translate the head.

q: What contributes to the effective depth of the glenoid socket?
a: The glenoid labrum, with additional passive stability from the capsule and ligaments.

q: State the key concept about what the cuff does.
a: The cuff is a compressor before it is a mover. It does not simply rotate the humerus — it generates compressive forces that maintain joint stability throughout movement.

q: Why would deltoid fail without the cuff?
a: In the early arc deltoid's line of pull is largely vertical. Without cuff compression holding the head centred, deltoid would drag the head superiorly against the acromion instead of rotating it about a fixed point.

q: How much superior translation occurs during normal elevation?
a: Only about 1–2 mm. The centre of rotation stays remarkably still.

q: Which long-taught claim about supraspinatus should be abandoned?
a: That it "initiates the first 15° of abduction." It is active across the whole arc, its dominant function is compression, and many patients with isolated supraspinatus tears abduct fully.

q: What does cuff dysfunction produce — and what does it not?
a: Loss of the fulcrum: painful, inefficient, substituted movement with a shrugging pattern. Not frank paralysis. Significant loss of the fulcrum is characteristic of large or massive tears, not simple tendinopathy.

q: Describe the coronal force couple and the consequence of its failure.
a: Deltoid's superior pull balanced by the inferior cuff (lower subscapularis, infraspinatus, teres minor). Failure gives unopposed deltoid → superior migration, loss of fulcrum, pseudoparalysis in the extreme.

q: Describe the transverse force couple and why it matters for tears.
a: Subscapularis anteriorly balanced by infraspinatus and teres minor posteriorly. This is the couple that must stay balanced for a tear to remain functional. Imbalance gives anteroposterior instability during rotation.

q: What are the four mechanical contributions of the scapula?
a: Upward rotation (keeps the glenoid under the head), posterior tilt (elevates the acromion away from the cuff), external rotation (maintains the glenohumeral relationship), and a stable base for the cuff's origin.

q: What is the single fact that justifies scapular training?
a: The cuff originates on the scapula. A muscle cannot produce stable compression if its origin is unstable.

q: What limits the argument for scapular training?
a: Scapular dyskinesis is common in asymptomatic people and its association with pain is weaker than commonly taught. Train the scapula because the symptom-modification test was positive, not because it looked unusual.

q: How common is scapular dyskinesis in athletes?
a: A systematic review of 12 studies and 1,401 athletes found it in roughly 55–61% of overhead athletes and 33% of non-overhead athletes — though it did not separate symptomatic from asymptomatic participants.

q: What is the scapular plane, and why do we test and load in it?
a: The scapula sits about 30–45° anterior to the coronal plane. In that plane the capsule is relatively untwisted, the cuff has favourable lines of pull, and there is less soft-tissue impingement than in pure coronal abduction.

q: State the scapulohumeral rhythm.
a: Elevation to 180° is roughly 120° glenohumeral and 60° scapular upward rotation — a 2:1 ratio. For every 3° of arm elevation, about 2° is glenohumeral and 1° scapulothoracic.

q: What is the caveat to the 2:1 ratio?
a: It is a teaching approximation, not a constant. Contributions vary with phase, plane, load, speed and individual. The first 30° is predominantly glenohumeral, with the scapular contribution increasing through the arc.

q: Define moment arm, and state the shoulder's mechanical disadvantage.
a: The perpendicular distance from a muscle's line of pull to the joint's centre of rotation. The arm is a 60–70 cm lever while the muscles acting on it have moment arms of only 2–3 cm — roughly a 20:1 disadvantage.

q: How much muscle force does holding 1 kg in the hand require?
a: Something like 20–30 kg of muscle force, because of the 20:1 mechanical disadvantage.

q: How heavy is the arm, and what joint reaction force does holding it horizontally generate?
a: The arm is about 4–5% of body weight (3–4 kg). Held out horizontally with nothing in the hand, the glenohumeral joint reaction force approaches body weight.

q: What do instrumented shoulder prostheses record for joint reaction force during elevation?
a: Peaks ranging from roughly 50% to over 170% of body weight, depending on the individual and how far they elevate.

q: Name the four factors that multiply cuff demand.
a: 1) Elevation angle — demand rises steeply from the side toward 90°. 2) Lever length — straightening the elbow roughly doubles torque. 3) External load — multiplied by the 20:1 disadvantage. 4) Time — sustained overhead positions accumulate load and fatigue the cuff.

q: Why is a long shift often more provocative than a heavy lift?
a: Sustained overhead positions accumulate load and fatigue the cuff, degrading compression exactly when it is most needed.

q: Give the position-based progression ladder that needs no change in weight.
a: Supine → supported upright → scaption below 90° → full range → overhead → overhead with time under load.

q: Why is unloaded range-of-motion work not a null stimulus?
a: In an irritable shoulder, moving the arm's own weight is a real load. A 4 kg arm at 90° of elevation is a meaningful demand for a deconditioned tendon — which is why supine is often the right place to start.

q: What is the fastest dial for regressing an exercise?
a: The elbow. Bending it halves the torque, regressing the exercise without the patient feeling they have gone backwards.

q: State the capacity–load model.
a: Symptoms arise when the demand placed on the tendon exceeds its current capacity to tolerate that demand. Both sides of the mismatch are modifiable.

q: Name the three stages of the continuum model.
a: Reactive → dysrepair → degenerative.

q: What characterises a reactive tendon, and how should it be loaded?
a: The tissue is already over-responding, with cells in an exaggerated state of activity. Load it heavily and you drive that response further. Reduce load, use isometrics as a tolerable way of keeping it loaded, give it one to three weeks, then build.

q: What characterises dysrepair?
a: The tendon has tried to repair and it is going wrong — more cells, more proteoglycan, collagen separating and losing alignment, early new vessels with nerve fibres alongside. Weeks to months of symptoms, with the aggravating activity usually continuing throughout. This is where you have the most to gain.

q: What characterises a degenerative tendon, and what is the main treatment error?
a: Established breakdown — areas of cell death, disorganised matrix, extensive neovascularity; those areas are not coming back. The main error is underdosing, usually because a scan report frightened someone.

q: Explain the doughnut and the hole.
a: The degenerate area is the hole and will not be restored. Most of the tendon's cross-section is doughnut, and that tissue adapts perfectly well. You are not repairing the hole — you are strengthening the ring.

q: How do you stage a patient on the continuum in practice?
a: Not precisely — you cannot biopsy them and imaging cannot reliably stage them. You assess irritability: how little it takes to provoke, how long it takes to settle, and whether there is rest or night pain. That maps onto the continuum closely enough to be useful.

q: What is the commonest presentation in a PM&R clinic, and why does it matter?
a: "Reactive-on-degenerative" — an older tendon with established degenerative change, acutely overloaded. A long background of niggling discomfort punctuated by a recent sharp deterioration. Treat the reactive component first.

q: What is the single commonest reason a well-intentioned programme flares and the patient disengages?
a: Going straight to heavy loading in a reactive-on-degenerative tendon.

q: Why is "tendinitis" the wrong word? Name the histological features.
a: The tissue shows degenerative, not inflammatory, change: collagen disorganisation with fibre thinning and loss of crimp; increased ground substance and proteoglycan with water uptake; neovascularisation with accompanying neural ingrowth.

q: Why does pain often begin in the dysrepair stage?
a: The tissue is acquiring a nerve supply it does not normally have, as new vessels grow in with nerve fibres alongside them.

q: Which structure is probably the biggest contributor to pain, and why?
a: The subacromial–subdeltoid bursa. It is synovial, densely innervated, sits directly on top of the tendon and under the arch, and in cuff disease thickens, becomes irritated and is compressed every time the arm elevates.

q: State the conceptual point about pain underneath the whole chapter.
a: Pain is an output, not a tissue readout. It is produced by the nervous system weighing nociceptive input together with context — expectation, threat value, sleep, mood, what someone has been told about their scan.

q: Why can two people with identical imaging have completely different experiences?
a: Because pain is an output of the nervous system weighing input against context — which is also why the consultation itself changes outcomes.

q: Describe the load–pain relationship in a typical tendon problem.
a: A given activity produces a reasonably reproducible amount of pain, often with a characteristic 24-hour latency — worse the next morning rather than during the activity.

q: What does it mean when pain is unpredictable, unrelated to load and widespread?
a: You are no longer managing a pure capacity problem. The programme must still be loaded, but it needs pacing, education about sensitisation, sleep management and often psychological input — and progress will be measured in a different currency.

q: How should night pain be framed and used?
a: Characteristic, not alarming. It responds to positioning more reliably than to analgesia, and is worth tracking as an outcome — "how many nights a week does it wake you?" is sensitive and patient-meaningful.

q: Why do tears propagate rather than heal?
a: Before the tear, load was spread across the full width of tendon. The fibres that carried that share are gone, so the same external load produces higher local strain at the tear margin. The edge is the weakest point and is being asked to carry more.

q: Why do bigger tears enlarge more readily than small ones?
a: A larger defect concentrates more strain at its edge.

q: Name the two routes to a rotator cuff tear.
a: Degenerative — capacity drifts down over years until the tissue fails under loads it used to tolerate; insidious, often no clear event. Traumatic — a single event exceeding the capacity of relatively normal tissue.

q: Why does the degenerative-versus-traumatic distinction matter?
a: It determines the management split. A traumatic tear in a younger patient warrants early surgical referral; a degenerative tear found in an older patient usually gets a loading programme.

q: Describe the characteristic pain of rotator cuff tendinopathy.
a: Lateral deltoid pain, often poorly localised, sometimes radiating to the deltoid insertion but rarely below the elbow.

q: What is the classic painful arc?
a: 60–120° of elevation.

q: What is often the most disabling single feature?
a: Night pain, especially lying on the affected side.

q: Which functional losses do patients typically report?
a: Difficulty with overhead and behind-the-back activities — a high shelf, washing hair, fastening a bra, reaching a back pocket, a seatbelt.

q: What is the nature of weakness and stiffness in cuff tendinopathy?
a: Weakness, if present, is often pain-inhibited rather than structural. Stiffness is mild and end-range — global stiffness points elsewhere.

q: Which history question outperforms all others, and why?
a: "What were you doing in the month before it started?" rather than "what happened?". Patients report the moment pain appeared; tendons respond to the preceding accumulation, three to six weeks upstream.

q: Define irritability and name its three components.
a: How much it takes to provoke, how severe it gets, and how long it takes to settle.

q: Describe high irritability and its starting approach.
a: Pain at rest; night pain every night; provoked by minimal activity such as dressing or light reaching; takes hours to settle; active range limited by pain well before passive end-range. → Settle first: isometrics, pain-free range, sleep positioning, activity modification, consider a short NSAID course or an injection as a window. Avoid provocative loading for 1–3 weeks.

q: Describe moderate irritability and its starting approach.
a: Pain with moderate activity; some night pain; settles within an hour; active range near passive. → Load cautiously but genuinely: light-to-moderate isotonic loading through tolerable range, 2–3 sets, progress every 1–2 weeks.

q: Describe low irritability and its starting approach.
a: Pain only with heavy or sustained load; no night pain; settles quickly; full range. → Load properly: heavy slow resistance, higher loads, add range, add speed. Underdosing is now the main risk.

q: Why is irritability the single most practically useful assessment?
a: It sets the dose. Diagnosis sets the direction; irritability sets the dose — and unlike the diagnosis, it changes week to week.

q: Why must active and passive range be compared?
a: The relationship between them is the structural discriminator. Preserved passive range with limited active range points to the cuff; loss of both points to the capsule.

q: What should be used to measure range, and what should not?
a: An inclinometer, goniometer or smartphone application — graded A in the 2025 guideline. Not visual estimation. Scapular range measures are unreliable and should not be used for dynamic scapular ROM.

q: What does a lag sign indicate, and what are its test properties?
a: Loss of force transmission — probable structural tear. You removed the demand to move and the unit still could not hold position. Lag signs are specific but not sensitive: a positive is far more informative than a negative.

q: Why is the full can preferred over the empty can as a loaded exercise?
a: Comparable supraspinatus activation with less subacromial narrowing and less provocation. The empty can retains a role as a test (Jobe's), not as an exercise.

q: What should replace manual muscle testing, and why?
a: Hand-held dynamometry — grade A in the 2025 guideline. Manual testing cannot detect the side-to-side deficits and incremental gains that tell you whether capacity is rising.

q: What is the normal ER:IR ratio?
a: Roughly 0.65–0.75. A value well below this is a specific, trainable posterior cuff deficit.

q: What is the real diagnostic value of the provocation tests?
a: Modest. Combinations improve accuracy only marginally over single tests, and the reference standards in the accuracy studies were surgical findings in secondary-care populations — not tendinopathy as defined clinically.

q: Which two tests have the best diagnostic value, and for what?
a: Painful arc to confirm; Hawkins-Kennedy to rule out (grade B). Both likelihood ratios are small, so do not rely on test results alone.

q: Why can rotator cuff special tests not be interpreted in a stiff shoulder?
a: They are all positive when the capsule is tight and everything hurts at end range. This is a common source of a wrong second diagnosis.

q: What should you watch during scapular assessment, and why?
a: The lowering phase, not just the lift — control fails eccentrically first.

q: Name the scapular tests worth performing.
a: Scapular assistance test and scapular retraction test; wall press or push-up plus for serratus integrity; pectoralis minor length (supine, how far the acromion rests off the plinth); thoracic extension available in sitting.

q: What makes scapular work earn a place in the programme?
a: A scapular assistance or retraction test that changes this patient's symptoms — not an unusual appearance.

q: What four questions must the examination answer?
a: Is it the cuff at all? Is there structural failure? How irritable is it? What is the target load?

q: What is the single most useful product of symptom-modification testing?
a: The specific position and load that was comfortable in clinic — which becomes the first exercise, written in those words. The patient leaves having already succeeded at it once in front of you.

q: What does global loss of passive range, with external rotation lost first, suggest?
a: Adhesive capsulitis — a different condition with a different plan. Passive range is the discriminator.

q: What does painless weakness suggest?
a: Neurological causes — suprascapular neuropathy, C5 radiculopathy, neuralgic amyotrophy, motor neuron disease. Tendinopathy weakness hurts.

q: What does severe pain preceding patchy weakness suggest?
a: Neuralgic amyotrophy.

q: Why screen the cervical spine every time?
a: C5 radiculopathy often has no neck pain at all. Waiting for the patient to complain of their neck is how it gets treated as cuff disease for months.

q: What does bilateral shoulder girdle pain with marked morning stiffness in an older patient suggest?
a: Polymyalgia rheumatica — check ESR/CRP.

q: What should abrupt, severe, out-of-keeping shoulder pain prompt?
a: Consideration of acute calcific tendinopathy — the radiograph shows the deposit.

q: When is "not yet" a defensible answer to imaging?
a: Almost always at first presentation. The guideline recommends against imaging to confirm rotator cuff tendinopathy initially; consider it if symptoms have not resolved within a maximum of 12 weeks of appropriate non-surgical management.

q: In a population-based MRI study of 602 adults aged 41–76, what proportion had a cuff abnormality?
a: 98.7% — only 1.3% were normal. Tendinopathy 25%, partial-thickness tear 62%, full-thickness tear 11%. Just 18% reported current symptoms.

q: How did abnormality rates compare between symptomatic and asymptomatic shoulders in that study?
a: 96% of asymptomatic versus 98% of symptomatic — a difference of 1.8% (95% CI −2.9 to 4.7). Essentially no difference.

q: What proportion of full-thickness tears in that study were in shoulders with no symptoms?
a: 78% (75 of 96). The apparent association between full-thickness tear and symptoms disappeared after adjusting for clinical examination findings.

q: Below what age were no full-thickness tears found, and why does that matter?
a: 45. A full-thickness tear in a younger patient is traumatic until proven otherwise. Prevalence rose from 4% at 45–49 to 28% at 70+.

q: Which imaging modality should be prioritised, and why?
a: Ultrasound — lower cost with diagnostic properties similar to MRI for confirming a cuff disorder. It is also dynamic, allows bilateral comparison, and can guide injection in the same sitting.

q: How do ultrasound, MRI and MR arthrography compare for full-thickness tears?
a: Essentially equivalent — MRI 94%/93%, MRA 94%/92%, US 92%/93%; no significant difference (p = 0.7). For partial-thickness tears, none performs well.

q: What is the magic angle artefact and how do you test for it?
a: Where supraspinatus curves over the humeral head its fibres sit near 55° to the main magnetic field, producing artificially increased signal on short-TE sequences (T1, PD, gradient echo). Real pathology persists on long-TE T2; magic angle signal disappears.

q: Which part of the MRI report carries the most prognostic weight?
a: The Goutallier grade — fatty infiltration is largely irreversible, and grades 3–4 predict poor functional recovery after repair. Read the muscle before the tendon.

q: State the Goutallier grades.
a: 0 normal muscle; 1 some fatty streaks; 2 fatty atrophy under 50%; 3 around 50%; 4 over 50%.

q: State the Cofield tear-size categories.
a: Small <1 cm; medium 1–3 cm; large 3–5 cm; massive >5 cm (also commonly, ≥2 tendons).

q: State the Patte retraction stages.
a: Stage 1 — stump close to the bony insertion. Stage 2 — at the level of the humeral head. Stage 3 — at the level of the glenoid.

q: State the Ellman grades for partial-thickness tears.
a: Grade 1 <3 mm (~<25%); grade 2 3–6 mm (~25–50%); grade 3 >6 mm (>50%). Located as articular-sided, bursal-sided or intrasubstance.

q: Which partial-thickness tear location is most common, and which is easiest to miss?
a: Intrasubstance tears are the most common in cadaveric studies — and the hardest to see.

q: What are the four targets of treatment?
a: Settle the symptoms, build capacity, restore the task, and change what the patient believes about their shoulder.

q: What is the governing principle of treatment?
a: Load is the treatment. Everything else buys a window — judge every adjunct by whether it lets the patient load sooner, heavier or more consistently.

q: Name the five education messages.
a: Capacity not damage · loading is the treatment · pain is allowed within the rule · months not weeks · the scan finding is normal for your age.

q: How should the condition be explained to a patient?
a: As a mismatch, not damage — the tendon has been asked for more than it can currently give. Name their own spike. Say that both sides of the mismatch can be changed. Avoid drawing the acromion, which teaches impingement.

q: What is the pain rule given to patients?
a: Up to about 5/10 during the exercise · settled by the next morning · not rising week to week.

q: Where does the pain rule come from, and what is the caveat?
a: Silbernagel's pain-monitoring model in Achilles tendinopathy. Patients who kept loading within these limits did no worse than those who rested six weeks, and the resting group gained nothing. No equivalent rotator cuff trial validates the thresholds.

q: How do you check that education has landed?
a: Don't ask "does that make sense?". Ask what they will tell their partner is wrong, what they will do if it is sore on Thursday, and when they think they will be back to normal.

q: What does the 2025 guideline grade A, and what does it deliberately omit?
a: Prescribing an active rehabilitation exercise programme as initial treatment, which may include motor control and/or resistance training with various loads — notably without specifying the dose, because the trial evidence does not support specifying it.

q: Which exercise type is clearly superior?
a: None. Eccentric, concentric, isometric and heavy slow resistance show no clear superiority for rotator cuff related shoulder pain. You are applying principles of tissue adaptation, not choosing between protocols.

q: How does non-progressive or non-resisted exercise perform against sham?
a: No significant benefit (pain MD −0.33/10, 95% CI −0.81 to 0.15). Progressive resisted exercise does reduce pain (MD −1.07/10). The active ingredient is progression and resistance.

q: What is "failed physiotherapy" usually?
a: A failed dose, not a failed treatment. Ask: what load were they actually lifting, how often, and did it ever increase? Four sessions of pendulums and a yellow band over six weeks is not a trial of rehabilitation.

q: Name the four phases and their main objectives.
a: 1) Initial loading — control symptoms, establish tolerable loading. 2) Progressive strengthening — improve cuff and scapular strength. 3) Advanced strengthening — load tolerance, endurance, overhead capacity. 4) Return to activity — restore occupational or sporting demands.

q: What are the approximate timeframes, and how should they be read?
a: Weeks 0–2, 2–6, 6–12, and 12 onward. Illustrative, not validated milestones. The stages are states, not weeks: patients enter on criteria, phases overlap, and a patient can move backwards after a flare.

q: Who needs stage 1, and who does not?
a: For a genuinely irritable shoulder — pain at rest or at night, provoked by light or brief activity, taking hours to settle, recently flared. Most patients do not need it. Starting everyone here delays treatment by three weeks and teaches the patient their shoulder is fragile.

q: Is the goal of stage 1 to eliminate pain before starting exercise?
a: No. The goal is to establish a level of loading the patient can perform consistently without sustained symptom exacerbation. Isometrics are an option, not a mandatory first stage.

q: What is the evidence for isometrics as an analgesic?
a: Weak. The original 4.3-point effect came from six athletes; follow-ups found 1.8, then 0.9, then −0.3 points. A meta-analysis of 10 trials and 294 participants found isometrics not superior to isotonic exercise. Use them because they are tolerable, not because they switch pain off.

q: Give a typical stage 1 isometric dose.
a: 5 holds × 30–45 seconds at about 70% effort, 30–60 seconds rest, once or twice daily. Progress the hold angle toward the provocative range before moving on.

q: What arrives in stage 2 that was absent in stage 1?
a: Movement through range, the eccentric (lowering) phase, and exposure to the whole available arc. Expect more symptom response in the first fortnight here than anywhere else.

q: Give a typical stage 2 dose.
a: 3–4 sets × 10–15 reps, about 3 s out and 3 s back, 60–90 s rest, three times weekly, at a load where the last 2–3 reps are genuinely hard.

q: Why does slow tempo matter?
a: It removes momentum so the muscle does the work; it makes the eccentric deliberate rather than a drop; it increases time under tension; and it is self-limiting — a weight that cannot be lowered over three seconds is too heavy.

q: How do you set the starting load?
a: Find a weight they can complete 15 controlled reps with, where the last two or three are hard. If 15 is easy it is too light; if they cannot reach 10 with control it is too heavy.

q: What should change when 3 × 15 becomes comfortable?
a: The load goes up — not the repetitions. Creeping to three sets of twenty-five converts strength work into endurance work.

q: Which progression within the programme is most often forgotten?
a: Moving external rotation from 0° out to 45°, then 90° of abduction. ER strength at the side does not transfer to ER overhead, and abduction with external rotation is the position patients most avoid.

q: Name the core exercises of stage 2 and the reason for each.
a: ER at 0° (the measurable deficit and the force-couple partner balancing deltoid's superior pull) · scaption/full-can (the elevation task itself, in the plane the shoulder is built for) · row (posterior chain and scapular control under real load) · press, landmine → incline → overhead (reaching the overhead task by angle rather than avoidance).

q: What is the commonest failure of a cuff programme?
a: The load never changes. A patient doing three sets of fifteen with a yellow band in week two should not still be doing that in week eight. At every review ask: what are you lifting now, and what were you lifting last time?

q: State the entry criteria for stage 3.
a: 3 × 15 comfortable at a meaningful load; full available range trained including the formerly provocative arc; ER loaded in abduction; no next-morning flare; irritability low — the limiting factor is now strength, not pain.

q: Name the four goals of stage 3.
a: 1) Close the strength deficit against the uninvolved side. 2) Build tolerance to heavy load near end range. 3) Build endurance and repetitive load tolerance. 4) Introduce faster and more complex movements.

q: Which exercises characterise stage 3?
a: Overhead press, ER at 90° abduction loaded, row, pull-down → pull-up progression, bench or incline press, loaded carries (including overhead carry), heavier scaption/lateral raise.

q: Why must ER work be kept in during stage 3?
a: It is the specific deficit, and no compound lift trains it.

q: Name the seven training variables that can be progressed.
a: Resistance, repetitions, shoulder position (side → elevated → overhead), lever arm, movement speed, complexity (isolated → integrated, multiplanar), and work capacity.

q: Who needs stage 4, and who does not?
a: Needed by those whose work or sport demands speed, elasticity or repeated overhead power — overhead athletes, manual workers applying force quickly, anyone facing rapid or unpredictable loading. Not needed by a 70-year-old whose goal is a kitchen shelf, or a desk worker who can press, row and carry at full load. For them, stage 3 is the finish line.

q: What two things deliberately do not change between stages 2 and 3?
a: The tempo and the frequency. The slow eccentric is as important at 6RM as at 15RM, and three sessions a week with real load beats five with compromised load.

q: When should a programme be regressed?
a: Symptoms not settling within 24 hours; morning pain or stiffness worse week on week; the patient compensating (shrugging, trunk lean, holding breath) to complete reps.

q: How should a flare be handled?
a: Reduce load by 20–30% and rebuild, rather than stopping. A flare means the dose exceeded current capacity — the correct response is a smaller dose, not no dose. Tell the patient this at the first appointment.

q: Why is stopping the wrong response to a flare?
a: It teaches the patient that loading is dangerous, costs the capacity already gained, and usually means starting again two weeks later from a lower baseline.

q: Why ask the patient to record their load?
a: It makes progression visible when pain is not yet improving; it tells you at review whether the dose actually increased; and it converts an abstract instruction into a measurable behaviour. It is also the quickest way to find out that a "12-week trial" involved the same green band throughout.

q: Give the troubleshooting sequence for a programme not working at 6–8 weeks.
a: 1) Is the diagnosis right? 2) Has the load actually increased (the commonest finding)? 3) Is it being done? 4) What is happening outside the programme? 5) Is the tendon reactive? 6) Is the background hostile (HbA1c, smoking, sleep, thyroid, weight, mood)? 7) Is sensitisation dominant? 8) Only now consider imaging and procedures.

q: What should a written programme contain?
a: Exercise, position, load, sets and reps, tempo, days, the pain rule, the progression criterion, the review date, and baseline numbers. Anything less is a suggestion.

q: How should every adjunct be judged?
a: By whether it lets the patient load sooner, heavier or more consistently. Load treats the cause; adjuncts treat the week.

q: What is the one-line summary of the physical modalities evidence?
a: Shockwave and laser are for the calcium, not the tendon.

q: What does the guideline recommend about therapeutic ultrasound?
a: Should not be used — grade C in calcific disease, grade B in non-calcific, alone or added to rehabilitation.

q: Where does extracorporeal shockwave therapy have a role?
a: Calcific tendinopathy only (grade C). It is recommended against for non-calcific disease. Caveat: Cochrane (32 trials, 2,281 participants) found effects below clinical importance and no calcific-versus-non-calcific subgroup difference.

q: Where does laser therapy have a role?
a: Calcific tendinopathy only (grade C), alone or added to an active rehabilitation programme.

q: What is the grade and role of manual therapy?
a: Grade B — spinal and/or upper limb manual therapy, alone or combined with exercise, for short-term pain reduction. Use it in the same session as the loading, as the thing that makes the next exercise tolerable.

q: What are the grades for taping and acupuncture?
a: Taping grade D (short-term pain reduction, conflicting evidence); acupuncture grade C, added to an active rehabilitation programme.

q: What is the role of corticosteroid injection?
a: May be used (grade B) for pain and short-term disability, but not first-line (grade C). Benefit is short term only — up to about 8 weeks — with no difference at medium or long term, and exercise beats it in the medium term.

q: Should corticosteroid injection be guided?
a: Yes where available (grade B) — though the effect of guidance is small (MD −0.58/10) and probably not clinically important.

q: What is the best-supported procedural option for calcific disease?
a: Ultrasound-guided lavage (barbotage) — grade B, for calcific tendinopathy refractory to initial treatment. It outperformed shockwave for both pain and calcification size in the long term.

q: What are the grades for PRP and hyaluronic acid?
a: Both grade D, and both explicitly not first-line (grade F). A network meta-analysis of three high-quality RCTs found no significant pain reduction with hyaluronic acid versus placebo at any time point.

q: For which interventions is there insufficient or conflicting evidence to recommend either way?
a: Prolotherapy, suprascapular nerve block, stem cell injections and botulinum toxin.

q: What did the CSAW trial find?
a: Arthroscopic subacromial decompression was no better than placebo arthroscopy at 6 months (Oxford Shoulder Score −1.3, 95% CI −3.9 to 1.3). Both beat no treatment, but below the 4.5-point target difference.

q: What did FIMPACT find at 5 years?
a: No clinically relevant benefit of decompression over placebo surgery, and none over exercise therapy. The authors recommended replacing the term "shoulder impingement" with "subacromial pain".

q: What does Cochrane conclude about subacromial decompression?
a: High-certainty evidence of no clinically important benefit over placebo for pain, function or quality of life at one year. The review does not support the operation.

q: What does Cochrane conclude about surgery for rotator cuff tears?
a: Probably little or no meaningful benefit over exercise with or without injection at 12 months. No placebo-surgery trial has ever been done, and most participants had small degenerative supraspinatus tears — so it does not speak to traumatic or large tears.

q: What does Cochrane conclude about electrotherapy modalities?
a: Ultrasound, low-level laser and PEMF added to exercise produce no clinically important additional benefit (47 trials, 2,388 participants).

q: What pattern runs through the Cochrane evidence on this condition?
a: The negative findings are the high-certainty ones; the positive findings sit at low to very low certainty.

q: Which patient-reported measures are suitable, and what does the guideline grade this?
a: SPADI, DASH/QuickDASH and ASES are named as suitable options. Using valid, reliable and responsive questionnaires is graded A.

q: Give the approximate MCIDs for the common shoulder measures.
a: SPADI ≈8–13 points · QuickDASH ≈8–15 · ASES ≈12–17 in cuff disease · Oxford Shoulder Score ≈4–6 · WORC ≈11–13% · Constant–Murley ≈10 points.

q: How should MCID values be treated?
a: As approximate thresholds for "the patient would notice this", not precise cut-offs. They vary between studies and populations. Choose one measure and use it consistently.

q: What limb symmetry index is targeted before return to heavy or overhead demand?
a: Greater than 90%, measured on handheld dynamometry in a standardised position.

q: Give the physical benchmarks for discharge.
a: Range symmetrical with the other side (inclinometer, not visual estimate) · ER, IR and scaption strength LSI >90% · ER:IR ratio roughly 0.65–0.75 · endurance matched to occupational demand · the actual provocative task completed without next-day flare.

q: When should measurements be taken, and why three points?
a: Baseline, 6 weeks and 12 weeks, the same way each time. Three points answer the only question that matters: is capacity rising? If pain is unchanged but ER strength has risen 30%, the programme is working and needs time.

q: Why does "better" fail as an outcome?
a: It will not survive a clinic letter, a return-to-work discussion or an insurance query.

q: On what timeline does tendon adapt, and when do patients feel better?
a: Adaptation on roughly a 12-week timeline; patients feel better at about six. That gap is where relapse happens — say so in advance.

q: How do you answer "shouldn't I get a scan?"
a: "We can, and sometimes we should. But at your age the scan will almost certainly show some wear, which is also true of people with no pain at all. It would change what you believe more than what we do. If you're not improving in about twelve weeks, that's the point at which the scan starts to earn its place."

q: Which factors most strongly predict persistent pain?
a: Age over 55 (OR ~3.8) and perceived high job demand (OR ~4.1). Also delayed care after injury, prolonged symptoms and a compensation or litigation context.

q: What is the status of psychological factors as predictors in this condition?
a: They predict outcome in surgically managed patients, but the evidence does not support them as predictors in conservatively managed shoulder pain. Address distress because it affects adherence, not because it determines outcome.

q: Which commonly assumed factors do not predict persistence?
a: Dominant versus non-dominant side, education level, comorbidities, pressure pain thresholds, perceived job control, and jobs requiring higher shoulder forces.

q: What must accompany discharge?
a: A maintenance prescription — 1–2 strength sessions weekly, indefinitely, for anyone with ongoing overhead demands, including ER work. Capacity decays, and a patient discharged with nothing returns to the state in which they broke down.

q: The painter: a middle-aged decorator after three weeks of ceiling work. What is the key management move?
a: Identify the spike and modify it with an expiry date — platform or extension pole to bring work to chest height, alternate ceiling and wall work, cap continuous overhead time — while loading begins.

q: The fall: what distinguishes this presentation and changes the pathway?
a: Trauma with marked weakness or a positive lag sign, particularly in a younger patient, warrants early surgical referral rather than three months of rehabilitation first.

q: The incidental tear: what is the teaching point?
a: This case is won or lost in the explanation. If she leaves believing her shoulder is broken and waiting for a repair, no programme will be done properly.

q: The thrower: 22-year-old javelin athlete, six months of posterior pain in late cocking, 25° IR deficit, positive scapular assistance test, no lag signs, two steroid injections each helping a month. Why is he at risk?
a: He is the patient most likely to be under-rehabilitated — he will feel fine at the end of stage 3 and return to full throwing. The relapse happens in week two of the season.

q: Pearl 1 — what replaces the impingement model?
a: "Impingement" is an outdated causal model. Think capacity versus load.

q: Pearl 3 — what sets the dose, and what sets the direction?
a: Irritability sets the dose; diagnosis sets the direction.

q: Pearl 4 — what is the cuff, functionally?
a: A compressor first. Dysfunction is loss of a fulcrum, not loss of one movement.

q: Pearl 9 — how should an imaging report be weighted?
a: Imaging findings are age-related and common. A tear on a scan is not a diagnosis, and the report changes beliefs more than management.

q: Pearl 12 — what is the commonest cause of a failed programme?
a: A dose that never progressed.

q: Pearl 13 — what does a flare mean?
a: A smaller dose, not no dose.

q: Pearl 14 — what is the surgical position?
a: Subacromial decompression did not beat placebo surgery. Repair for the right tear still has a role, and a traumatic tear in a younger patient should be referred early.

q: Pearl 15 — what follows a massive irreparable tear?
a: Not the end of rehabilitation. The anterior deltoid programme restores useful function in many patients.

q: List the red flags.
a: Acute traumatic tear with marked weakness or a positive lag sign in a younger patient → early surgical referral. Weakness without pain → neurological (suprascapular neuropathy, C5 radiculopathy, neuralgic amyotrophy, motor neuron disease). Severe pain preceding patchy weakness → neuralgic amyotrophy.

q: What is the line that summarises the whole chapter?
a: You finish on a number, not a feeling.
